stem: Which TWO controls are preventive rather than deterrent? (Choose two.)

options.text: Bollards across the vehicle approach
options.why: A vehicle physically cannot pass. The attacker's intent is irrelevant, which is what makes it preventive.

options.text: An access control vestibule
options.why: It physically stops a second person following the first through the door.

options.text: A sign reading 'These premises are under video surveillance'
options.why: A sign persuades. Anyone who ignores it walks straight past, so it deters and prevents nothing.

options.text: Security lighting across the car park
options.why: Lighting makes an attacker feel exposed. It blocks nobody.

options.text: A corporate acceptable use policy
options.why: A policy is directive in type and managerial in category. It instructs, it does not prevent.

stem: An access point is being configured for WPA3-Enterprise. Which TWO are required for clients to authenticate at all? (Choose two.)

options.text: A reachable RADIUS server
options.why: In Enterprise mode the access point only relays credentials. Without a RADIUS server nothing can make an authentication decision.

options.text: An EAP method configured on both the AP and the clients
options.why: 802.1X carries EAP. Without an agreed method there is no authentication exchange to carry.

options.text: A pre-shared passphrase of at least 12 characters
options.why: A shared passphrase is WPA3-Personal. Enterprise authenticates each user individually and has no PSK.

options.text: SSID broadcast disabled
options.why: Hiding the SSID is obscurity and is irrelevant to whether authentication succeeds.

options.text: MAC filtering populated with every client address
options.why: MAC filtering is a separate, trivially bypassed control. It is not part of 802.1X.

stem: Which TWO combinations qualify as multifactor authentication? (Choose two.)

options.text: A smart card plus the PIN that unlocks it
options.why: Something you have plus something you know. Two categories, so it is multifactor.

options.text: A fingerprint plus a hardware security key
options.why: Something you are plus something you have.

options.text: A password plus a security question
options.why: Both are something you know. Two prompts, one factor.

options.text: A password plus a PIN
options.why: Also both knowledge. This is the exam's favourite fake second factor.

options.text: A fingerprint plus a retina scan
options.why: Both are something you are. Two biometrics are still one factor.

stem: Which TWO log patterns most strongly suggest a credential has been compromised rather than a user mistyping? (Choose two.)

options.text: Two successful logins from cities 9,000 km apart, 20 minutes apart
options.why: Impossible travel. Both succeeded, so this is not a typing problem.

options.text: The same account active in two sessions simultaneously from different networks
options.why: Concurrent session usage. One person cannot be in two places.

options.text: Twelve failed logins on one account followed by a lockout
options.why: That is brute force or a stale saved password. Nothing succeeded, so no credential is proven compromised.

options.text: One failed login against each of 300 accounts
options.why: That is password spraying, an attack in progress rather than evidence a specific credential is already compromised.

options.text: A password reset requested by the user through the help desk
options.why: A routine event. On its own it indicates nothing.

stem: A worm is spreading and legal has asked for a full forensic investigation. Which TWO actions belong to containment and preserve evidence? (Choose two.)

options.text: Disconnect the affected hosts from the network, leaving them powered on
options.why: Stops the spread while memory, processes and connections survive for acquisition.

options.text: Block the worm's port between workstation subnets at the switch
options.why: Network segmentation stops lateral movement across every host at once, and touches no evidence.

options.text: Power off every affected host immediately
options.why: Contains the spread and destroys every byte of volatile evidence, which legal has just asked for.

options.text: Reimage the affected hosts from a known good image
options.why: Reimaging is eradication, it comes later, and it destroys the evidence.

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan on every workstation
options.why: Scanning is eradication one host at a time while the worm keeps reinfecting from neighbours.

stem: Which TWO properties does a digital signature provide? (Choose two.)

options.text: Non-repudiation
options.why: Only the holder of the private key could have produced it, so they cannot later deny it.

options.text: Integrity
options.why: Any change to the signed content invalidates the signature.

options.text: Confidentiality
options.why: Signing leaves the content in plaintext. To keep it secret you must also encrypt it with the recipient's public key.

options.text: Availability
options.why: Signatures have nothing to do with keeping a service reachable.

options.text: Key exchange
options.why: Key exchange is a separate operation. A signature proves origin, it does not establish a shared key.

stem: A company's backups were encrypted by ransomware along with production. Which TWO design properties would have preserved a usable copy? (Choose two.)

options.text: An offline copy the production systems cannot reach
options.why: Ransomware can only encrypt what the compromised host can write to. An air-gapped copy is out of reach.

options.text: Immutable storage where written objects cannot be altered for a retention period
options.why: Even with credentials, the attacker cannot overwrite an object under an immutability lock.

options.text: Continuous replication to a second data centre
options.why: Replication copies the encryption as faithfully as it copies the data. It protects against site loss, not corruption.

options.text: Encrypting the backup files at rest
options.why: That protects their confidentiality. The ransomware encrypts them again regardless.

options.text: Running the backup job twice as often
options.why: More frequent copies to a reachable share means more encrypted copies.

stem: Which TWO characteristics identify malware as a worm rather than a virus? (Choose two.)

options.text: It propagates across the network without any user action
options.why: Self-propagation with no user involvement is the defining worm behaviour.

options.text: It is a standalone program that needs no host file
options.why: A virus attaches to a host file. A worm does not need one.

options.text: It encrypts files and demands payment
options.why: That is a payload. Either type can carry it, so it does not classify the malware.

options.text: It hides itself from security tools
options.why: Concealment describes a rootkit, which is a separate category.

options.text: It arrives disguised as useful software the user installs
options.why: That is a trojan, and it requires exactly the user action a worm does not need.

stem: Outbound filtering must let only PROXY-01 reach the internet on 443. Which TWO rules violate least privilege even though the required traffic still works? (Choose two.)

options.text: permit tcp CORP-NET any -> any 443
options.why: The whole internal network gets outbound HTTPS, which is exactly the path malware uses to call home.

options.text: permit tcp PROXY-01 any -> any any
options.why: The right source and every port. The proxy can now reach anything, not just the web.

options.text: permit tcp PROXY-01 any -> any 443
options.why: This is the correct rule: one named source, one destination port, written in the direction the connection is initiated.

options.text: deny ip any any at the bottom of the list
options.why: An explicit deny at the end permits nothing. It exists so the drops get logged.

options.text: permit udp DNS-SRV any -> APPROVED-DNS 53
options.why: A separate, correctly scoped rule for a different requirement. One source, one destination, one port.

stem: Which TWO outputs come from a business impact analysis rather than a risk assessment? (Choose two.)

options.text: Recovery time objective for each business process
options.why: The BIA establishes how long each process can be down, which sets the RTO.

options.text: Maximum tolerable downtime per function
options.why: Also a BIA output, derived from how long the business survives without the function.

options.text: A register of threats with likelihood ratings
options.why: Likelihood of a threat is a risk assessment output. The BIA is deliberately indifferent to cause.

options.text: Annualized loss expectancy for a named asset
options.why: ALE comes from quantitative risk analysis, not from the BIA.

options.text: The organisation's stated risk appetite
options.why: Appetite is set by the board as a strategic posture, not produced by either exercise.

stem: A medical device runs an operating system the manufacturer will not patch and cannot be replaced this year. Which TWO are appropriate compensating controls? (Choose two.)

options.text: Place the device on an isolated VLAN reachable only by the one server it must talk to
options.why: The control you wanted is unavailable, so network isolation meets the objective another way. That is what makes it compensating.

options.text: Monitor the segment and alert on any traffic outside the one permitted flow
options.why: Detection substitutes for the prevention you cannot deploy, and it is recorded against the documented exception.

options.text: Apply the latest vendor patch
options.why: The scenario states there is none. This is the control that is unavailable, which is why a compensating one is needed.

options.text: Accept the risk and record it in the register with no further action
options.why: That is acceptance, not compensation. Acceptance leaves the exposure exactly as it was.

options.text: Install endpoint protection agents on the device
options.why: An unpatchable legacy OS generally cannot run a current agent, which is part of why it needs isolating.

stem: Reviewing a suspected intrusion, which THREE findings are indicators of compromise rather than ordinary operations? (Choose three.)

options.text: A security log with no entries for a 45 minute window while the host was running
options.why: A running host generates events. A gap is positive evidence something removed them.

options.text: A signed Microsoft binary loading a DLL from a user's AppData directory
options.why: Legitimate binaries do not normally load code from a user profile. This is the classic living-off-the-land pattern.

options.text: Outbound connections to one host on a fixed 60 second interval for nine days
options.why: Machine-regular timing to a single destination is beaconing, not human browsing.

options.text: A server showing sustained high CPU and slow response
options.why: A symptom of load. It is as likely to be a victim of the incident as a participant in it.

options.text: An antivirus full scan completing with zero detections
options.why: A clean signature scan proves nothing when the technique has no signature. It is not itself an indicator.
